primitives.name: Temporal Stability Index
primitives.verbatim_quote: Specifically, we develop methods to evaluate metrics based on three criteria: (1) stability: does the metric measure the same thing over time (2) discrimination: does the metric differentiate between players and (3) independence: does the metric provide new information?
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'X_{spm}': 'Random variable representing metric value for player p in season s for metric m', '\\mathcal{S}_m': 'Stability index for metric m, dimensionless'}
primitives.assumptions: Player performance is modeled as a random variable with finite variance; temporal consistency implies low within-player variance relative to total variance.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When \( \mathcal{S}_m \to 0 \), metric loses stability; when \( \mathcal{S}_m \to 1 \), metric is perfectly stable.

layer2.mapping: GSI uses \( \mathcal{S}_m \) as a prior in Bayesian update of player ability estimates; GSE encodes \( \mathcal{S}_m \) into transition probabilities of player state graphs.
layer2.telemetry: Repeatability coefficient across seasons, variance ratio of player-level vs total variance.

primitives.name: Player Discrimination Score
primitives.verbatim_quote: Specifically, we develop methods to evaluate metrics based on three criteria: (1) stability: does the metric measure the same thing over time (2) discrimination: does the metric differentiate between players and (3) independence: does the metric provide new information?
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'X_{spm}': 'Metric value for player p in season s for metric m', '\\mathcal{D}_m': 'Discrimination score for metric m, dimensionless'}
primitives.assumptions: Higher variance between players indicates better differentiation capability; assumes fixed player ability over time for comparison.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When \( \mathcal{D}_m \to \infty \), metric perfectly discriminates; when \( \mathcal{D}_m \to 0 \), metric fails to distinguish players.

layer2.mapping: GSI applies \( \mathcal{D}_m \) to rank players probabilistically; GSE uses it to weight feature importance in multi-metric decision trees.
layer2.telemetry: Inter-quartile range of metric values across players, ratio of between-to-within variance.

primitives.name: Metric Independence Coefficient
primitives.verbatim_quote: Specifically, we develop methods to evaluate metrics based on three criteria: (1) stability: does the metric measure the same thing over time (2) discrimination: does the metric differentiate between players and (3) independence: does the metric provide new information?
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'X_{m_1}, X_{m_2}': 'Metrics m1 and m2 values for same player-season combination', '\\mathcal{I}_{m_1,m_2}': 'Independence coefficient between metrics m1 and m2, dimensionless'}
primitives.assumptions: Metrics are jointly normally distributed; independence implies zero correlation.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When \( \mathcal{I}_{m_1,m_2} \to 0 \), metrics are highly dependent; when \( \mathcal{I}_{m_1,m_2} \to 1 \), metrics are independent.

layer2.mapping: GSI treats \( \mathcal{I}_{m_1,m_2} \) as mutual information in multivariate Gaussian model; GSE uses it to prune redundant features in ensemble models.
layer2.telemetry: Pearson correlation coefficient between two metrics, adjusted for shared variance.

reasoning_traces.think:
The core insight of meta-analytics lies in decomposing metric utility into three orthogonal dimensions: stability, discrimination, and independence. Stability is quantified via the ratio of between-player variance to total variance, capturing temporal consistency. Discrimination is measured by the ratio of between-player to within-player variance, assessing the metric’s ability to distinguish players. Independence is captured through the correlation coefficient between pairs of metrics, indicating redundancy. These primitives form a triadic framework for evaluating and constructing metrics. Failure modes include metrics with low stability (e.g., noisy short-term stats), poor discrimination (e.g., uniform player scores), or high dependence (e.g., overlapping indices). Dualities emerge in that stability and discrimination are inversely related in some contexts—highly stable metrics may lack discriminatory power, and vice versa. The framework supports a principled approach to metric selection and synthesis, particularly in high-dimensional spaces where combinatorial explosion of metrics threatens decision clarity.
